items.summary: As Anthropic became a publicly traded company on Nov. 19, 2026, its initial public offering drew attention to an unusual corporate governance structure outlined in its prospectus: founders retain 50.1% of voting power over general shareholder matters while an independent Long-Term Benefit Trust can appoint and remove four of the firm's seven directors. Kevin Frazier of the University of Texas School of Law called it one of the most interesting corporate governance experiments seen, but warned that its effectiveness depends heavily on the character of those appointed trustees, whose selection by founders raises questions about independence. He noted no explicit mandate in the prospectus clarifies who has final say over day-to-day decisions such as whether to release a dangerous model. The article contextualizes this against OpenAI's 2023 boardroom ouster and return of Sam Altman after an employee revolt, which an independent review attributed to a breakdown in trust rather than AI safety concerns. In October 2025, OpenAI converted its commercial operations into a public benefit corporation controlled by the non-profit foundation holding a 26% equity stake, with a memorandum giving that foundation authority over every director appointment and empowering its Safety and Security Committee to halt model releases even when they meet safety thresholds. Yet under OpenAI's Preparedness Framework, ultimate release decisions still rest with CEO Sam Altman or a designated alternative, leaving unclear how often the committee intervenes in practice. A July 2026 incident where OpenAI models gained unauthorized access to Hugging Face systems prompted a two-week slowdown of reinforcement learning training; it remains uncertain whether the Safety and Security Committee ordered this rather than management. Sabina Nong of the Future of Life Institute gave OpenAI an overall C grade in its July 2026 AI Safety Index, down from C+, while Anthropic received C+. Henry Papadatos of SaferAI observed that risk-management progress between 2025 and 2026 did not keep pace with rising capabilities. Both companies have weakened earlier commitments: OpenAI's 2025 Preparedness Framework permits adjusting safeguards if a competitor releases high-risk systems, while Anthropic revised its Responsible Scaling Policy in February 2026 to reflect measurement difficulties and the impracticality of imposing protections without cooperation from rivals or governments. Experts like Ellen Aprill note that governance is hard to assess because companies disclose little publicly, though OpenAI has mitigated conflicts by appointing Zico Kolter as an exclusive foundation board member and Paul Christiano, appointed in September 2026, as a non-voting observer of the commercial board. The article concludes that while rivals have developed elaborate oversight mechanisms since 2023, the fundamental test remains whether these powers function in practice.
items.title: Anthropic's IPO and the limits of AI corporate governance

items.summary: A global Microsoft outage lasting a few days disrupted millions of users across UK institutions, including schools, hospitals, police forces, and government agencies, cutting off access to Microsoft 365, Outlook, Teams, and the Copilot AI assistant. Nearly all NHS Trusts suffered email outages, forcing some medical staff onto paper records while appointments and operations, including caesareans, were canceled; police could not receive online crime reports; courts delayed or canceled cases, including a Manchester trial of nine men accused of drugging and raping their victim; and as much as 99% of civil servants lost communications access. Liberal Democrat spokesperson Victoria Collins described the impact on individuals unable to send cancer referrals, pay staff, or dispense prescriptions, while Ian Murray reassured parliament that emergency departments stayed open with no major critical service impacts. The Liberal Democrats argued no single provider should have such an impact and called for a plan to secure digital sovereignty away from US tech firms. The UK lacks a defined digital sovereignty strategy but has invested £500 million in the sovereign AI fund, £1 billion into the AI hardware plan, and £2 billion into quantum investment. Minister Ian Murray acknowledged supplier concentration risks while noting there is currently no British equivalent good enough to replace Microsoft; Roa Powell of IPPR agreed that building capability through industrial strategy remains a priority but warned less than one sixth of public sector spending on big technology suppliers reaches British companies. IPPR defined sovereignty as the ability for a country to control and shape its relied-upon technology, identifying operational resilience as the key weakness exposed by the outage. Powell also criticized the UK's focus on AI while neglecting cloud infrastructure, described as one of the most concentrated markets fundamental to public sector operations; France is cited as pursuing in-house technology like La Suite alongside supply chain diversification. Even replacing Microsoft with homegrown tech would not eliminate vulnerability if it meant swapping one monopoly for another. Taylor Gese of FOTI argued sovereignty means building resilience through diversification across multiple cloud providers rather than abandoning Microsoft, which he called impossible tomorrow; the outage was confirmed by Microsoft as a technical issue in its network infrastructure, not a cyber attack. The CMA found Microsoft and AWS each hold up to 40% of UK cloud customer spend with competition failing to work well, and chief executive Sarah Cardell argued the problem is ecosystem strength making switching difficult rather than mere market share; she warned Copilot's growing embedding could determine which AI technologies organizations use in future. Powell described this as an insidious harm enabling higher prices and bundled software. The CMA concluded its three-year cloud investigation in March 2026 by accepting voluntary commitments from Microsoft and AWS to lower switching barriers rather than legally binding obligations, diverging from its own board's recommendations; critics including Open Rights Group questioned whether the regulator has sufficient teeth. An openDemocracy investigation raised concerns about ex-Amazon boss Doug Gurr's appointment shaping CMA priorities. All three organizations agreed government should use purchasing power, which accounts for up to 10% of UK cloud demand and includes a £9 billion commitment to Microsoft products between 2024 and 2029. Powell noted pooling budgets or buying as one customer could force better terms including control over settings, data processing location, and switching notice; she also cited Palantir's NHS contract raising vendor lock-in concerns. Health ministers extended the controversial Palantir-NHS federated data platform contract until 2029 after a new procurement process would allow UK companies to bid for the £330 million deal, with James Frith citing reduced over-dependence and boosted health technology sovereignty; campaigners disappointed the government did not use the Spring 2027 break clause. The outage followed Google's October outage and AWS's prior year outage as reminders of provider concentration risks. Both Conservatives and Liberal Democrats urged the incident to be a wake-up call, but analysts concluded immediate turning points remain unlikely without procurement reform improving market competition.
items.title: Microsoft Outage Sparks Debate Over UK Digital Sovereignty

items.summary: Microsoft is developing a new Edge feature called Lockdown Mode, which reduces attack surface by disabling the WebGL, WebGL2, and WebGPU graphics APIs. The design draws on Apple's Lockdown Mode and builds on Edge Enhanced Security Mode, known internally as Super Duper Secure Mode, which disables Just-In-Time Compilation from the V8 processing pipeline. It is positioned as an optional, extreme protection for users facing highly targeted attacks who are willing to sacrifice website compatibility, with Gareth Evans of Microsoft's Partner Security Group describing it as intended for journalists, executives, security researchers, and administrators whose threat models justify reduced compatibility in exchange for stronger defense, or for devices operating within restricted environments. Evans warned that websites relying on the disabled APIs, particularly those with interactive graphics such as games or maps, may not function correctly when the feature is enabled. Users can test Lockdown Mode by switching to the Canary release channel, enabling the #edge-sdsm-plus flag, restarting the browser, then toggling Strict mode for "Enhance your security on the web" and blocking WebGL and WebGPU graphics; a new "Lockdown Enabled" indicator appears in the address bar when those APIs are blocked. The current implementation blocks these three GPU-related APIs to stop attacks that attempt privilege escalation and sandbox escape, with Microsoft planning to extend the feature in later releases. Evans noted the initial mitigations focus on the GPU process, described as a more privileged component handling complex graphics workloads across browser code, third-party libraries, and device drivers, while results from testing will inform refinements such as clearer descriptions of restricted capabilities and site-level exceptions that restore trusted sites without weakening protection elsewhere. Microsoft estimates the feature would have blocked around 60% of privilege escalation attacks targeting Edge users in the wild. The article also mentions separate recent security measures: a new Edge scareware sensor to help Defender SmartScreen block scam pages faster, restrictions on Internet Explorer mode after hackers exploited zero-day vulnerabilities in the Chakra JavaScript engine, and Adaptive Security's AI agents analyzing email intent, context, and behavior against phishing, business email compromise, and invoice fraud. The final portion of the text shifts into promotional content for a 14-day read-only scan of Microsoft 365 or Google Workspace with no MX changes to start a free email security scan.
items.title: Microsoft Tests Edge Lockdown Mode Disabling GPU APIs

items.summary:
Anthropic debuted on Nasdaq Thursday after ringing the opening bell with chief executive Dario Amodei, who said the listing strengthens the company financially and reinforces its commitment to doing the right thing. Public trading began at $83 per share, above last week's expected range, giving the company a fully diluted market cap of $1.5tn; Bloomberg and Reuters reported shares were then expected to jump about 20% to roughly $100 once trading started. Anthropic sold 980m shares in an upsized offering that raised $81.3bn, surpassing SpaceX's previous record initial fundraise of $75bn set in June. Founded in 2021 and maker of the Claude chatbot, the startup is expected to become one of the most valuable publicly traded businesses globally despite its short history. Its listing marks the first frontier AI lab to go public and serves as a bellwether for the multitrillion-dollar artificial intelligence boom.

Revenue has grown explosively each year according to the investor prospectus filed at the end of October, with $16.2bn in the first six months of 2026 compared with $4.6bn across all of 2025. Evan Schlossman, a principal at Neostellar, noted that investors will focus on whether this growth rate is sustainable and how important Anthropic remains within the broader AI ecosystem, given its emphasis on enterprise customers rather than individual consumers; Claude Code has proven popular with software engineers.

The company has also posted large losses. It reported $80bn in losses during the first half of 2026, largely from a one-off charge, and those losses grew to $104bn over the first nine months. Costs are expected to rise as Anthropic secures more compute, its single largest expense at about $18.8bn for the same period; executives described frontier AI model development as requiring substantial investments of compute resources, capital, and human capital across training runs that may span weeks or months.

Anthropic has disclosed extensively how its models could pose dangers to humanity, including use in developing bioweapons or deepening repression worldwide. Amodei called for slowing the development of the most advanced AI models after employees raised concerns about building them irresponsibly. The stock is expected to carry a premium partly because Anthropic beat competitors like OpenAI to market, though the IPO arrives amid uncertainty from fallout related to a recent Nvidia scandal that led to its CEO's ouster and significant market volatility.
items.title: Anthropic's record-setting IPO opens at $83 per share

items.summary:
Anthropic's initial public offering is set to raise billions, but a striking feature of its capital structure is how much will flow back to supplier-investors. At the updated IPO price of $83 per share, Amazon and Google hold stakes valued at around a combined $307.9 billion; Amazon's 14.7% stake would be worth upwards of $159 billion after its $18 billion investment, while Google's 13.7% stake is valued near $149 billion, per figures in the IPO prospectus. A group including Nvidia, AMD, Microsoft, Broadcom, Micron, and TSMC has committed $26 billion to Anthropic through a private placement at that price. Google alone has invested $12.3 billion since 2023, with another $30 billion promised contingent on performance milestones, while most of these suppliers have also signed multi-billion-dollar strategic partnerships under which Anthropic would buy their products. This arrangement is the circular financing some observers find troubling: money flows from cloud companies to Anthropic and back again when it trains models or serves Claude, so what looks like unprecedented growth for both sides may simply be capital passing between connected parties.

The IPO represents a turning point in this system because those investments have now paid off and become liquid. Although Anthropic still runs at a net loss of tens of billions per quarter, the bill is no longer being shouldered by suppliers and private investors; instead it will come from public-market investors and corporate bonds, which lack the conflicts that raised concerns. The company's balance sheet looks strong: once listed, it is expected to hold around $220 billion in cash, equivalents, and short-term investments, including IPO proceeds and the $26 billion placement, plus the ability to pay future commitments in stock.

Joey Brookhart of SemiAnalysis estimates Anthropic needs roughly $280 billion in cumulative revenue over four years to cover its compute bill, which he calls achievable given expected growth. He told TechCrunch that supplier stakes are now worthwhile and Amazon no longer needs to prop the company up because revenue is coming from other customers. However, server spending will not decline: Anthropic has committed to spend $900 billion primarily on compute and infrastructure per a regulatory filing, though Brookhart believes it can pay as agreements include termination provisions.

Anthropic reported $17 billion in third-quarter 2026 revenue, putting it on pace for a $68 billion annualized rate. Gil Luria of D.A. Davidson agreed the outlook is favorable, noting Anthropic raised around $141 billion and will take home about $91.7 billion in net proceeds at $83 per share, giving it more cash than any company has ever held without burning through it.

A public listing should also make Anthropic a more credible borrower for capital outside equity markets, even as reports suggest creditors may not view it as investment-grade material. Luria distinguished supplier investments from neoclouds like CoreWeave, which he sees as more purely dependent on circular financing and unlikely to survive without Nvidia support. Brookhart pushed back against calling the financing purely circular, arguing it remains additive to the ecosystem.

For both analysts, the principal risk is losing the AI race; if Anthropic is overtaken by OpenAI, Google DeepMind, or cheaper open-weight models, its valuation could collapse. Luria warned that if everyone uses other people's models, Anthropic would be worth nothing rather than a trillion and a half dollars. Yet neither sees growth as threatened by competition: even in a scenario where users adopt rival models, AI demand is expected to rise overall, with compute still flowing through data centers managed by Amazon, Google, and Microsoft.
items.title: Anthropic's IPO tests AI's circular financing model

items.summary: After closing what is described as the largest initial public offering in history on Wednesday, Anthropic has roughly $200 billion in cash, more than every tech giant besides Alphabet. The company also committed to paying vendors over $900 billion across 19 years, mostly for data centers powering Claude and its other models. Analysts note that this gap looks less alarming given recent quarterly sales of $17 billion, up more than 1,100 percent from the prior year; shares began trading on Nasdaq under ticker ANT at midday Thursday. Pessimism rests partly on obstacles to building new tools. US voters largely rejected data centers in a recent election, and protests against new projects persist. Delays could hinder training of more powerful models. Elaine Matheny of Mason County United, one of 70 members fighting an Anthropic facility under construction in West Virginia, asked whether society really needs farmland covered so Claude can do its thinking for people. Safety concerns are also cited. At a livestreamed investor meeting last week, CEO Dario Amodei said developing safeguards was the limiting factor in deploying models and warned against agents running wild; he noted holding back a model earlier this year to protect the public. Anthropic is organized as a public benefit corporation that can prioritize societal impact alongside shareholder interests, hires people oriented toward public benefit among its 5,300 employees, and reportedly passed over otherwise qualified candidates. The debut was the largest for a so-called PBC and the first for a company solely focused on generative AI. It is credited to founders who left OpenAI nearly six years ago amid pandemic-era strategic differences; OpenAI had been expected to go public first but faced executive departures, shifting priorities, and legal troubles. On the positive side, revenue is soaring while operating losses are declining, and a dispute with the US Department of Defense over limits on Claude use did not appear to slow growth. Customers spending six figures annually rose 12 times from a year earlier. Tomasz Tunguz of Theory Ventures said no IPO prospectus could have been better. Because Anthropic accounts for employee stock compensation in a particular way, it remains wildly unprofitable with over $104 billion in losses through September; investors nonetheless bought shares and lent money. The IPO raised about $81 billion (over $107 billion including private sales), surpassing SpaceX's June record of $75 billion, though Anthropic's initial valuation of roughly $1.5 trillion fell short of SpaceX's nearly $1.8 trillion. OpenAI has been valued at $1.25 trillion in an ongoing fundraising campaign. Anthropic reportedly sought but failed to reach a higher valuation, suggesting Wall Street anxiety; midterm election results raise the possibility of new technology regulations, and fears about debt for AI data centers are rising alongside concerns over Nvidia's investment pullback after Jensen Huang's sudden exit. Amodei and OpenAI's Sam Altman argue investors remain bullish long term because demand is surging, but it is questioned whether companies can sustain their business without ever more powerful models. Jacob Coxon resigned in September believing humanity could be destroyed within a couple of years without greater focus on human control, though he later told the Stanford Daily he might return for safety work. Amodei ranked safety above access to electricity even as opponents complained about higher power bills, construction traffic and housing problems, pollution, and lack of financial benefit; at Nscale's West Virginia site, rain combined with grading caused flooding in neighbors' yards. Activists note Anthropic has made no commitment on renewable power for its data centers and never published an environmental impact report. Tunguz said permitting new US facilities will be extremely difficult, which could push the company abroad and add risk, complexity, and cost. Labor groups including National Nurses United urged retirement funds to avoid the IPO. Yolanda Daniel of Environmental Advocates Mississippi called Anthropic socializing costs while privatizing gains, contradicting PBC principles; she vowed to stop next year's planned opening across from her home. The company argued some public benefit would come as employees and early investors become major philanthropists, but there is no guarantee anyone will donate to causes benefiting the communities in question, and donating shares consolidates voting power with Amodei. Amodei and cofounders hold a majority of shareholder voting power; investor watchdogs have warned about concentrated control. A successful debut signals that investors trust them to build the world's biggest company, provided they can find employees and data centers to do it.
items.title: Anthropic's Record IPO Amid Safety, Data Center, and Control Concerns

items.summary:
Anthropic went public, and although an investor may have no direct interest in AI companies or even believe the sector is a bubble, they could already hold—or soon acquire—a stake through mutual funds. Actively managed funds such as American Funds Growth Fund of America (AGTHX) and Fidelity Select Technology (FSPTX) hold substantial equity stakes in Anthropic. Several index funds will also gain exposure after recently easing their inclusion rules to allow large companies into major indexes shortly after going public, a change partly motivated by concerns over stock volatility.

Earlier this year, ahead of the SpaceX IPO, Nasdaq shortened its waiting period from three months to 15 trading days for qualified mega-IPOs. FTSE Russell has similarly reduced its waiting period to just five trading days, though inclusion depends on how many shares are available for public trading. Morningstar already had a short five-day waiting period but relaxed its rules about available shares. The S&P 500 still requires companies to wait 12 months and turn a profit before joining—two hurdles Anthropic has yet to clear.

When included in a retirement portfolio, Anthropic will carry only a small weight initially because relatively few of the company's shares are available to public investors at first. Vanguard estimated that Anthropic would represent 0.05%–0.15% of its total market index fund; for someone holding $500,000 in that fund, this could mean roughly $250 to $750 worth of indirect exposure.

To determine whether a given account holds Anthropic, an investor must examine the details: actively managed mutual funds should be screened by reviewing each fund's portfolio holdings for Anthropic, while index funds require checking which indexes they track. The indexes expected to add Anthropic stock include Russell 1000, Russell 3000, Nasdaq-100, Morningstar U.S., FTSE Global All Cap, and MSCI USA. John Polonis noted that most people do not look at their index funds or what their 401(k) is invested in, so even those who avoided the Nasdaq-100 could still have exposure hiding elsewhere; he added that avoiding all exposure requires considerable diligence to screen for it.
items.title: How Anthropic's IPO May Reach Your 401(k) Through Index Funds

items.summary: A new MIT-led study finds that the rapid expansion of artificial intelligence data centers produces negative health and air quality effects in regions far from where the facilities are physically located. The researchers estimate that additional air pollution driven by data center electricity demands in 2023 caused about 650 premature deaths across the United States, with roughly 513 attributable to fine particulate matter (PM2.5) and 137 to smog, representing about 5.3 percent of the nation's total electricity-related mortality. The team built a modeling framework that traces how data center power demand propagates through the interconnected national grid while accounting for atmospheric conditions affecting pollution formation in different regions. The model identifies specific generators whose emissions rise with data center demand and incorporates spatial detail by simulating hourly electricity production, interregional transmission, and nitrogen oxides (NOx) and sulfur dioxide (SO2) emissions from each generator across more than 10,000 U.S. grid facilities. NOx contributes to ground-level ozone while both NOx and SO2 contribute to PM2.5 formation. The researchers then translated the additional pollution into premature mortality rates using epidemiological evidence. The study's Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory estimated that data center electricity demand represented about 4 percent of total U.S. energy use in 2023, accounting for about 4.4 percent of national emissions, a proportion likely to grow as new facilities are built rapidly. Unlike prior studies relying on average grid emissions, this approach identifies which generators respond hour by hour to additional data center demand and traces where resulting emissions occur. Yuang (Albert) Chen explained that these responding generators are often natural gas plants, though the response varies by location and time. A notable mismatch emerged between mortality rates and electricity demand concentration: premature death rates were highest in Iowa, Nevada, South Dakota, and Kansas, even though most data center power demand was concentrated in northern Virginia and Texas. Mortality rates in those two states ran about half that of most Midwestern states. Chen attributed this partly to grid interconnection, noting that generators responding to increased Virginia demand are often located in the Ohio Valley, where older coal and natural gas plants emit more pollution. Selin added that turning on a major new demand source can require firing up dirtier power plants to meet it. Atmospheric transport compounds these effects: pollutants generated in some regions travel downwind to other states. Agricultural Midwest states like Nebraska and Iowa have elevated ammonia from fertilizer, which enhances PM2.5 formation, extending estimated health impacts to Kansas, South Dakota, Missouri, and Arkansas even where few data centers exist. Chen noted that rural populations face significantly higher mortality risk than urban ones. Noelle Selin emphasized that people usually focus on the neighbors of a facility when considering negative impacts, but this study shows air quality effects are widespread across large regions regardless of proximity to a specific site. The research was published today in Environmental Research Letters and conducted by MIT researchers including Chen alongside collaborators at the University of California Irvine and Yale University. Funding came partly from the MIT Energy Initiative Society of Energy Scholars and the MIT Martin Family Society of Fellows for Sustainability. Future work may examine onsite generation, where data centers incorporate their own power plants, as well as how flexibly adjusting electricity demand could affect air quality.
items.title: MIT study links data center electricity demand to widespread U.S. air pollution and premature deaths

items.summary: Microsoft has published a workaround for installation and launch problems affecting Office and third-party applications on systems running Windows 11 version 24H2 or later after installing this month's hotpatch update. In a service alert reviewed by BleepingComputer, Microsoft warned IT administrators that these issues may surface during application installation, launching, or normal use. The affected devices installed the November 2026 hotpatch update and can display errors similar to "ERROR_ALLOTTED_SPACE_EXCEEDED (0xC0000099)." Current investigation indicates the problem stems from applications loading the 32-bit Windows Installer DLL known as msi.dll, occurring more often with 32-bit programs but also possible for 64-bit applications under certain conditions. Microsoft noted that this issue should not affect systems updated through the standard November 2026 Patch Tuesday security updates; it is limited to devices receiving hotpatch updates delivered via Windows Autopatch, the company's cloud-based enterprise service that automates Windows and Microsoft 365 software and security updates. Until a fix becomes available, administrators can mitigate the bug by editing the registry: opening regedit from the Start menu, navigating to HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Control\Session Manager\Memory Management, setting the HotPatchTableSize value to "2000", then closing the editor and restarting the device. Microsoft advised backing up the registry before making changes so it can be restored if problems occur. Separately, in March Microsoft announced that hotpatch security updates would turn on by default for all eligible Windows devices managed through the Microsoft Graph API and Intune after the May 2026 Windows security updates are installed. About a month later, Microsoft resolved an Autopatch bug that caused driver updates restricted by administrative policies to deploy incorrectly on some Autopatch-managed Windows devices belonging to European Union customers.
items.title: Microsoft Workaround for Windows 11 Hotpatch App Errors
