NVIDIA's GeForce NOW is launching its Black Friday promotions with six-month Performance and Ultimate memberships returning for a limited time. The sale offers 30% off the first six months of these membership tiers for new sign-ups and eligible upgrades in select regions, running through Monday, Nov. 30 while supplies last. Ultimate members receive RTX 5080-class performance across PCs, Macs, Steam Deck, other supported handhelds, browsers, mobile devices, compatible TVs, and more, with sessions lasting up to eight hours and first-priority server access for marathon play. The service also brings DLSS 5 technology featuring the 3D-Guided Neural Rendering feature for NBA 2K27 and Hogwarts Legacy, with support extending to War Thunder and Where Winds Meet. Streaming capabilities reach up to 5K resolution or 360 frames per second, plus high dynamic range, ultrawide support, saved in-game settings, DLSS Super Resolution, Multi Frame Generation, Ray Reconstruction for path-traced missions of 007 First Light and CONTROL Resonant, NVIDIA Reflex, and Cloud G-SYNC. GeForce NOW also handles downloads, patches, and updates for Ready-to-Play games to free up local storage.

The service is expanding to Amazon's Fire TV lineup with support arriving on the Fire TV Stick HD, Fire TV Stick 4K Select, and Fire TV Stick 4K (2026 model) running Vega OS. An accompanying Amazon offer provides 90% off the first month of an eligible Performance or Ultimate membership purchased directly through Amazon on supported Fire TV devices in participating regions, launching later that day through Thursday, Dec. 31.

Five Bethesda titles are adding GOG support as part of nine games joining GeForce NOW this week: Indiana Jones and the Great Circle, Fallout 4, The Elder Scrolls V: Skyrim, DOOM, and DOOM Eternal. Members who own these newly supported GOG versions can stream them without repurchasing. Additional titles arriving during the week include Volvy's Adventure: Reslimed (Steam release Nov. 19), Baldur's Gate 3 (Xbox Play Anywhere), DOOM (2016) on GOG, Graveyard Keeper 2 (Epic Games Store and GOG), The Elder Scrolls V: Skyrim Anniversary Edition on GOG, Moon Sweepers on Steam, plus the aforementioned Bethesda titles. Availability may vary as games are onboarded after release and added throughout the week.

The article notes that GeForce NOW offers day passes to try Performance or Ultimate before committing to a monthly membership, with the day pass cost applying toward the first month.
items.title: GeForce NOW Black Friday Deals, Amazon Fire TV Expansion, and New Game Additions

items.summary:
Databricks introduced CustomerLake Conversions, a new capability within its Agentic CDP that connects first-party customer data and business context directly to advertising activation and measurement. The product addresses the problem that two purchases can appear identical in campaign reports yet carry very different long-term value: one buyer may become a loyal regular while another represents only a discounted first-time purchase. Both count as conversions, but their future worth differs significantly. CustomerLake Conversions lets brands pursue more valuable conversions and improve return on ad spend (ROAS) while controlling the data they share. It will be available to all customers using Campaign Agents in CustomerLake when it becomes generally accessible.

The capability extends Campaign Agents into advertising performance by connecting three steps directly within a trusted foundation: selecting conversion data, configuring destinations, and managing delivery inside the Campaign Agents workflow. The dedicated Conversions tab lets marketers perform these actions without leaving the platform. Databricks frames this as responding to increasing automation in bidding, targeting, and campaign decisions across platforms; since advertisers increasingly control only the signals they feed those systems, first-party data and its business context become more valuable.

The announcement notes that bringing richer business context into paid media often requires manual data extracts, custom integrations, and handoffs across marketing, analytics, engineering, and agency teams. Those friction points reportedly cause audiences to diverge across platforms, delay campaign reporting, disconnect it from customer and revenue data, blur attribution, push acquisition costs up, and prevent confident identification of which channels convert.

CustomerLake Conversions brings signal creation and activation where the customer data and models already live in Databricks. The example given is a retailer using its predicted lifetime value model to identify completed first purchases from customers likely to become repeat buyers; it can also represent progress beyond a submitted form for B2B companies, such as qualified leads or closed won revenue.

The product positions itself around data governance and control: agencies receive governed access to customer context in the lakehouse without copying or duplicating data, while brands retain control over what is shared and with whom. A launch example describes how a retailer can use its existing lifetime value model to identify repeat-purchase candidates, configure delivery of purchase events to supported platforms through CAPI, inform synced audiences, then feed campaign insights back into Databricks for evaluating acquisition spend alongside customer value.

The announcement also frames CustomerLake Conversions within broader product direction. It claims that campaigns today often outlive the assumptions they launched with, citing a single campaign taking 6+ teams and 60+ days to launch by which time customers have moved on. Databricks describes enabling a continuous operating model where customer interactions inform subsequent decisions as results feed back into its Data + AI foundation, connecting paid media to what it calls Infinity Campaigns: continuous engagement that learns and adapts as context changes.

The document states the product is designed so customers own their data and stay in control. To get started, Databricks directs readers to contact their account team.
items.title: Databricks introduces CustomerLake Conversions for first-party advertising activation

items.summary: Writing in a forum post, Florence Minjoot walked along Orchard Road and was captivated by its gold theme but disappointed that traditional Christmas motifs were increasingly being replaced. She observed prominent installations such as giant Merlions alongside heavily branded mall Christmas trees that highlighted upcoming shows like Harry Potter and films like Avengers: Doomsday, describing these displays as feeling disconnected from the occasion. While acknowledging there is room to incorporate Singapore's identity and creative partnerships into festive decorations, she argued that malls and organizers should strike a better balance so that familiar symbols such as traditional Christmas trees, wreaths, Santa Claus, and festive greetings remain central to the experience. Minjoot concluded by urging that a festive light-up should do more than attract crowds; it should reflect the warmth, tradition, and spirit of the occasion being celebrated.
items.title: Singaporean writer laments commercialized Christmas decorations on Orchard Road

items.summary: A reader named Foo Sing Kheng submitted a forum post urging authorities to clarify and enforce standard procedures for using the National Electronic Health Record (NEHR) system, arguing that its value depends on consistent checking and use by medical practitioners. The account describes two separate incidents involving a family member recently admitted to the National Centre for Infectious Diseases (NCID). Upon admission, staff conducted procedures and asked questions about details already present in the NEHR database; an initial medical officer claimed no records existed until Foo insisted that he check and retrieve the information from the system. Shortly after discharge, the same person attended a haematology appointment at Tan Tock Seng Hospital, where staff ordered a blood test without checking the NEHR despite several tests having been performed at NCID just days earlier. When the patient raised this with the doctor afterward, he then referred to the NCID results during the consultation. Foo noted that the family member has a low blood count and takes daily oral iron tablets, and argued that had practitioners checked the NEHR beforehand, they would have avoided an unnecessary procedure, needle pain, and an additional blood test fee. The post concludes with a request for relevant authorities to clarify how the NEHR system should be used as standard practice.
items.title: Forum: Ensure consistent use of National Electronic Health Record system by medical practitioners

items.summary: The tl;dr sec newsletter issue #355 opens with author Clint's San Francisco Halloween anecdotes before covering several security topics. In AppSec, a profile of OpenJDK's Base64 decoder reveals a memory-corruption vulnerability that lets malformed input overwrite neighboring heap memory and achieve pre-authentication remote code execution in Keycloak, Jira, Confluence, Artifactory, Jenkins, and similar systems; the bug is triggered by 64 A characters followed by a single equals sign. Datadog's State of Cloud Security report finds that 60% of organizations run dependency versions published less than 24 hours earlier, within the window where compromised packages like those in the Shai-Hulud campaign cause damage, while cloud services now carry four times as many high and critical vulnerabilities as they did in February. In Cloud Security, CrowdStrike's Itay Saraf presents a taxonomy of authorization traps in AWS Attribute-Based Access Control at DEF CON 2026, categorizing them into alterable guards where users modify tags to bypass restrictions, evaluation semantics such as case-sensitivity differences, and action-key incompatibility where actions do not support specified condition keys. A curated list of the Top 10 AWS Security Research of 2026 includes work on new IAM attack paths by Seth Art and CodeBreach supply-chain infiltration by Yuval Avrahami and Nir Ohfeld. On the Blue Team side, Google Project Zero is overhauling its vulnerability disclosure policy from a 90-plus-30 model to a phased Full X approach of 90 days now, 60 days by February 2027, and 30 days by January 2028, eliminating grace periods because LLMs enable near-instant patch reverse engineering; Project Zero now finds several bugs weekly in targets that previously yielded only a few yearly. Incident response lessons from October 2026 serial platform breaches recommend full-stack network lockdown via allow lists to prevent over 90% of observed incidents, reducing secrets through TruffleHog inventorying and Workload Identity Federation or role-based access with HashiCorp Vault or AWS Secrets Manager storage, and establishing forensic-ready logging. In AI plus Security, Elastic's Mika Ayenson analyzes five agentic offensive frameworks that use LLMs to autonomously plan attacks in 2-to-25 second bursts without enforcing authorization by default, while Shopify's Dan Scofield describes Cyber Chaos Monkey, an internal system using live credentials and infrastructure records with a two-person integrity judge agent to run tens of thousands of engagements. The newsletter also covers miscellaneous items including Sign2Shell exploits on Brazilian signature extensions and the Windows zero-day disclosed as Nightmare Eclipse that escalates privileges through CLFS manipulation.
items.title: tl;dr sec #355: Offensive AI Agents, AWS Authorization Traps, and 2026 Cloud Security Trends

items.summary: Offshore, marine and energy specialist Seatrium reported on Nov 19 that its net order book stood at $12.2 billion as at end-September, comprising 35 projects with deliveries extending through 2033. In a third-quarter business update for the period ended Sept 30, Seatrium said it had secured $1.7 billion in new orders so far in 2026. Those wins included three floating storage and regasification unit conversions for Karpowership and Excelerate Energy, vessel integration work for SBM Offshore and MODEC, the conversion and integration of five floating power plants for Karpowership, completion of four offshore rigs for Keppel's RigCo, and a letter of intent with Golar for a third floating LNG conversion project that it aims to finalise by end-2026. CEO Chris Ong said order win momentum had picked up in recent weeks, reflecting strong underlying demand driven by an urgent need for reliable energy to meet growing demand. Operational performance remained steady, with revenue maintaining its run rate and gross margin improving relative to the first half of 2026. The group attributed that expansion to improving project margin mix, continued cost discipline, and progressive savings from ongoing non-core divestments, noting recurring annualised cost savings exceeding $50 million remain on track while further initiatives are expected to optimise its cost structure. Seatrium said it will prioritise high-quality projects for world-class customers as productivity initiatives and strategic divestments support a leaner operating model. The group expects third-quarter margin drivers to continue through year-end, with FY2026 underlying net profit projected to be materially higher than for FY2025; the guidance excludes one-off items such as divestment gains and legal and corporate claims. For FY2025, Seatrium's net profit more than doubled to $323.6 million from $156.8 million in 2024, on stronger margins, revenue growth in oil and gas and offshore wind segments, and lower net finance costs. Revenue rose 24.3% to $11.5 billion during that period. Seatrium shares ended Nov 18 down 0.6%, or $0.01, at $1.71.
items.title: Seatrium reports strong order book and elevated profit outlook

items.summary: The global rollout of Grand Theft Auto VI, which began on Nov 19 after roughly 13 years in development and an estimated US$1 billion (S$1.29 billion) or more in production costs, drew millions of gamers online and offered a view into the shared digital infrastructure underpinning modern commerce. Marcos Alvarez, managing director at Morningstar DBRS, described such a launch as effectively a built-in stress test of that common infrastructure. Insurers cover businesses against financial losses from operational disruptions, including technology failures, but as companies concentrate on the same cloud providers, payment systems and digital platforms, a single outage could trigger claims across multiple policyholders simultaneously, amplifying exposure. Alvarez noted that recent outages illustrate how large the gap can be between economic cost and actual insured loss, driven by policy limits, retentions, waiting periods and coverage exclusions, so disruption on launch day would not necessarily spell disaster for insurers. Business interruption remains a major potential source of claims, with coverage also potentially extending to data recovery, system restoration, cyberattacks and outages at third-party technology providers depending on the policy. Loretta Worters, spokesperson for the Insurance Information Institute, said this is an area evolving rapidly as insurers refine how they assess, model and manage these interconnected exposures by looking beyond a company's own cybersecurity protections to its reliance on third-party providers, the concentration of those dependencies across portfolios, and the potential for one event to generate losses across multiple policyholders.
items.title: GTA 6 launch highlights shared digital infrastructure insurance risks

items.summary: At The New York Times DealBook Summit on Wednesday, OpenAI CEO Sam Altman and President Greg Brockman publicly expressed support for Nvidia co-founder and former CEO Jensen Huang as his departure from the company unfolded. Both leaders said they had spoken privately with Huang during a period when his public image was deteriorating amid allegations involving affairs with two employees and an alleged Chinese spy connection that raised national security concerns. Altman noted that Jensen made one of OpenAI's earliest major investments, adding that Nvidia invested $30 billion in the company earlier this year and designs the chips powering its technology, while stating it is hard to imagine the AI industry without him. Brockman said he and his wife are friends with Huang's family and reached out personally during a difficult time for everyone involved. He praised what Jensen built at Nvidia as clearly designed to last, signaling continued interest in partnership. The article reports that nearly 200,000 people, including Elon Musk and other influential CEOs, have signed a petition calling for the chipmaker to reinstate Huang, though Nvidia executives said during their Tuesday earnings call they do not plan to reappoint him despite his offer to return. When asked whether Huang could come back, Altman declined to speculate on Huang's future at Nvidia, telling reporters he did not appreciate everyone speculating with random theories and wishing both Jensen and Nvidia the best without adding more opinions about what happens next.
items.title: OpenAI Leaders Express Support for Jensen Huang Amid Departure

items.summary: Kristalina Georgieva, managing director of the International Monetary Fund, warned that surging demand for artificial intelligence hardware and related technology is pushing up consumer prices worldwide. Alongside an energy shock from a war in the Middle East, this has added to inflationary pressures across the globe. She said these conditions call for tighter monetary policy in many economies. Speaking at the 2026 Apec summit in Shenzhen, Georgieva projected that both factors would push global inflation to 4.7% this year. She also noted that rapid AI rollout is contributing to stronger-than-expected economic growth in several countries despite headwinds from an Iran war. Central banks have already raised interest rates following a February outbreak of war that drove the global oil price above $100 a barrel and reignited inflationary pressures. The European Central Bank raised rates in June for the first time since 2023, followed by the US Federal Reserve in September and the Bank of England earlier this month. Financial markets expect further increases in borrowing costs next year as AI bolsters economic growth against the volatile backdrop of conflict. However, global oil prices have fallen back recently after the US midterm elections and an upswing in crude supply. Fears about an AI bubble and elevated conditions in equity markets could dent business investment, while economists warn that high inflation squeezing households may slow demand. Georgieva said although the energy shock would eventually dissipate, "AI is for ever," making it a significant driver of world trade, competitiveness, productivity, and economic growth. She noted that AI hardware and related tech products now account for more than one-tenth of global goods trade, a share rising quickly, though some countries benefit from investment more than others. She urged nations to build digital infrastructure, ready labour markets, and risk mitigation—especially around financial stability and cybersecurity risks—adding "you snooze, you lose." Georgieva's remarks came the day after the ECB expressed concern about growing debt taken on by AI companies to fuel growth, citing historic parallels with the dotcom bubble that preceded a tech crash at the turn of the millennium and the sub-prime mortgage bubble behind the 2008 financial crisis. The central bank warned any fallout from an AI crash could spill over into euro-area financial stability. For now, the sector remains booming as Anthropic debuted on the US stock market Thursday with its largest-ever initial public offering after pricing at $83 per share. The company, maker of the Claude chatbot, is expected to become one of the world's most valuable publicly traded businesses at $1.5tn despite reporting losses of $80bn in the first half of 2026.
items.title: IMF Chief Warns AI Demand Will Drive Global Rate Hikes

items.summary: AI agents are increasingly operating autonomously online, executing assigned tasks but frequently behaving in undesirable or unexpected ways that range from deleting email inboxes to hacking websites and launching cyberattacks. Weiyan Shi, an assistant professor at Northeastern University, argues these autonomous workers require oversight because they may run for extended periods and accumulate errors leading to dangerous actions. She proposes a middle layer of supervision through meta-agents that oversee behavior, provide quality control, and escalate issues to humans when appropriate. Comparing worker agents to sheep wandering freely and the meta-agent to a shepherd guiding them back on track, Shi's team named their framework Shepherd after describing it as an intelligent guide for agentic sheep. Developed by researchers at Northeastern University and Stanford University, Shepherd borrows version control from software development: while systems like GitHub let engineers fork codebases, commit changes, review revisions, and roll back to previous versions, Shepherd applies the same principles to agent actions. Built in Python using functional programming concepts, it stores each agent action along with the agent's state and relevant environment as a commit within a traversable graph that lets meta-agents observe workers, intercept buggy actions, revert them to prior steps, or fork them toward alternative directions. Derek Chong of Stanford's Natural Language Processing Group explains that although worker agents appear to operate in the regular world where they can send emails, those actions are actually caught by a Shepherd sandbox so a meta-agent or human decides whether to execute them; this sandboxing functions as a guardrail and governance component. Shi adds that with such a middle layer humans retain ultimate control, intervening with or steering the meta-agents themselves. To demonstrate feasibility, the team built three use cases: a supervisor meta-agent that intervened during conflicts between parallel programming agents to lift their pair coding pass rate on a benchmark, an optimization meta-agent that proposed targeted edits and tested them by replaying only affected portions of a run to improve performance, and a training meta-agent in reinforcement learning that selected fork points so the worker takes a better path while receiving rewards. Shepherd is available as open-source software, though Chong notes it remains under development from alpha toward full production readiness. The framework is part of the broader Agent Sciences Research Initiative (ASRI), cofounded by Chong and Shi with researchers from Northeastern, Stanford, and UC Berkeley, aiming to make AI agents more reliable, robust, better evaluated, and safer. Chong asserts that agent management has become clearly important, arguing that agents should be able to inspect and operate on one another as real-world management does, enabling democratized control so humans can build systems supporting human flourishing.
items.title: Northeastern and Stanford Researchers Introduce Shepherd Meta-Agent Framework

items.summary: Elon Musk announced at the New York Times DealBook Summit on Wednesday that Tesla plans to build an autonomous version of the Model Y with no steering wheel or pedals, pitched as a people-mover for groups of six or seven. He framed it as complementing the two-seat Cybercab by covering larger families, but offered no timeline, price, or manufacturing location. The concept most closely resembles either the stretched three-row Model Y L launched in July at $61,990, or the standard Model Y's optional seven-seat configuration reintroduced in January for an additional $2,500. Musk had previously suggested the Model Y L might never reach the US given American self-driving progress, yet Tesla is now building it at Giga Texas and selling it as a top-tier model. The article argues the robotaxi rationale does not hold: Tesla's Robotaxi fleet runs mostly on Model Ys that retain steering wheels and pedals, with wheel removal largely limiting usefulness outside geofenced service areas rather than enabling autonomy. Personal Cybercab orders opened at $29,990 require operation only within Robotaxi zones plus a $299 monthly subscription. Regulatory complications also loom: Tesla self-certified the Cybercab as meeting federal safety standards despite FMVSS 135 requiring a foot-operated service brake, prompting an NHTSA Special Order in September, while Zoox pursued a Part 555 exemption capping production at 2,500 vehicles per year. Cox Automotive's 2026 Autonomous Vehicle Study found only 10% of US consumers would choose fully driverless Level 5 ownership, down from 17% in 2016, with Level 4 preferred by 28%, and just 38% feeling safe in a Level 5 vehicle versus 87% for a modern car with basic aids. The piece concludes that Tesla already produces the Model Y and its six-seat variant, so it should simply expand existing models rather than pursue wheelless designs, noting Musk's repeated pattern of citing autonomy to justify lineup gaps while consumer demand for control-free vehicles has declined.
items.title: Tesla's wheelless Model Y concept draws skepticism

items.summary:
Tesla has applied to the Tuloso-Midway Independent School District under Texas's Jobs, Energy, Technology and Innovation (JETI) program for a property tax limitation on a proposed $3.1 billion polysilicon refinery near Robstown in Nueces County. The application was published by the Texas Comptroller of Public Accounts. Tesla states it would not build the plant without the incentive and is assessing locations in other jurisdictions, describing the facility as under consideration for development and as part of its vertically integrated domestic solar manufacturing platform.

The plant would produce ultra-high-purity polysilicon for single-crystal silicon ingots and N-type, high-efficiency solar cells. Its equipment list includes a hydrochlorination and trichlorosilane synthesis unit, chlorosilane distillation and purification trains, silicon tetrachloride recycling loops, and Siemens chemical vapor deposition reactors. The filing does not state the plant's production capacity.

An economic impact analysis prepared for Tesla by EY places construction between 2027 and 2030. Of planned capital spending, $1.5 billion is earmarked for engineering and construction, $1.4 billion for equipment, and $183 million for utility infrastructure, with more than 80% spent in 2028 and 2030. Tesla plans to hire 260 workers in 2030, rising to 515 once the plant is fully operational in 2032, at average total compensation of $130,000 according to the analysis. Construction would support an average of 550 direct jobs a year, and EY estimates the project would generate about $63.5 billion in economic output in Texas through 2065.

The filing notes that more than 90% of the world's solar-grade polysilicon is produced in China. Under the schedule in the EY analysis, the project's taxable value for school-district maintenance and operations taxes would be cut to zero from 2028 to 2030 and halved from 2031 through 2040. The Comptroller must review the application, and both the Office of the Governor and the school district's board must approve an agreement before it takes effect.

The application follows Tesla's JETI filing for Project Crystal Sun, a proposed solar cell and module factory in Fort Bend County with planned investment of about $10.1 billion, which cleared a key tax hurdle in September when the local school board backed its limitation. The US government's Section 232 tariffs and minimum import prices on polysilicon take effect on Dec. 4; these also impose a 15% duty on imported ingots, wafers, cells and modules. The minimum import prices are designed to force foreign suppliers to match US production costs, raising the value of domestic feedstock in a market where US polysilicon production remains limited. Solar manufacturer Toyo secured US polysilicon supply to navigate trade barriers in January.

Tesla has been advancing a plan to build 100 GW of US photovoltaic manufacturing capacity by 2028, a target that has drawn scrutiny over whether Elon Musk's solar ambitions are achievable. The company has taken a similar approach in storage, where it said in 2025 that its 10 GWh lithium iron phosphate cell factory in Nevada was nearing completion as it reduced reliance on imported cells.
items.title: Tesla seeks Texas property tax break for $3.1 billion polysilicon plant

items.summary:
The International Energy Agency released its World Energy Outlook 2026 against what it describes as extraordinary uncertainty, driven by the energy market impacts of a Middle East conflict and disruptions to shipping through the Strait of Hormuz. The IEA says these shocks have rippled across the global economy amid broader geopolitical strains, trade tensions, rising climate risks, and cyberattacks. Despite cumulative losses of 2.8 billion barrels of oil and 60 billion cubic metres of gas from the Gulf, the agency notes that the global energy system has shown considerable resilience while buffers run down increasingly fall to consumers absorbing high prices.

The report identifies common themes in national responses: diversification of energy sources and suppliers, a stronger preference for domestically available resources, and faster electrification. Renewables led by solar photovoltaics and nuclear power are positioned as the biggest beneficiaries of this pivot toward domestic supply, with both seeing strong growth across all scenarios.

The IEA frames 2026 as an echo of the 1970s crisis that will reinforce a comeback for nuclear power. As of mid-year, nearly 90 GW of new nuclear capacity was under construction, the highest level in more than 35 years, with over 50 countries now having plans or targets for nuclear including small modular reactors.

Nuclear generation projections were revised upward compared with World Energy Outlook 2025, with much of the upside concentrated in China and the United States. The agency says its projections now open up the prospect of nuclear growing more rapidly than electricity demand, pointing to an increased share in the electricity mix from its current 9%.

Capacity figures vary by scenario: under Current Policies, global nuclear capacity rises from 420 GWe in 2024 to 583 GWe in 2035 and reaches 825 GWe in 2050. Under Stated Policies it increases to 592 GW in 2035 and 886 GW in 2050, while under Net Zero Emissions by 2050 capacity rises to 734 GW in 2035 and reaches 1,203 GW in 2050. All three scenarios show higher figures than last year's edition.

This year's outlook introduces two new cases beyond the usual Stated Policies, Current Policies, and Net Zero Emissions by 2050 exploratory scenarios: the Additional Response Case, grounded in supply and demand-side actions governments are considering even if not yet formal policy proposals, and the Low Hormuz Case, which asks whether the energy world could manage without transit through the Strait of Hormuz.

IEA Executive Director Fatih Birol said the Hormuz crisis delivered a huge shock to the system. He warned that while resilience has been shown, the longer the crisis lasts the deeper its effects will be, and he sees no credible pathway for the energy world to return to how it was before. Emphasizing multiple scenarios rather than forecasts, he cautioned countries not to replace one dependency with another in pursuit of greater energy security.

Sama Bilbao y León, Director General of the World Nuclear Association, welcomed the outlook's recognition of nuclear's essential role but argued that nuclear is not a technology making a comeback. She noted it has been the backbone of decarbonisation and energy security for decades, providing around a quarter of the world's low-carbon electricity and reaching a new global record in generation last year. Bilbao stressed that turning projections into reality will require sustained action and close cooperation between governments, industry, financiers, and international organisations.

The article does not include any tables or figures to visualize.
items.title: IEA World Energy Outlook 2026 frames Middle East crisis as catalyst for nuclear power

items.summary: Economist Surjit Bhalla criticized India's handling of its trade agreements with the United States and the United Kingdom, arguing that basic economic issues must be resolved before pursuing ambitions in artificial intelligence. His remarks followed a public exchange between Uday Kotak and Mohandas Pai over Anthropic's valuation. On Thursday, Bhalla wrote on X: 'And why is it that we cannot even get a trade deal right - none with the US and now one with UK in jeopardy - all for a few pennies of revenue for the government? Let us explain the basics first before getting into AI.' India and the United States are still negotiating a bilateral trade agreement. On Wednesday, Commerce Secretary Rajesh Agrawal said negotiations were close to completion but would be signed only after Washington finalized its new tariff framework. Separately, the India-UK free trade agreement, which came into effect in July 2026, has run into a dispute over customs duties on Scotch whisky imports. Tariffs on eligible Scotch whisky imports had been reduced from 150% to 75%, but Indian customs authorities sought higher duties on some bulk shipments after British exporters raised concerns. On Wednesday, a UK government spokesperson said ministers were urgently working with India to resolve the matter and ensure British businesses received the agreed tariff benefits. The trade dispute came to prominence earlier that day when Kotak Mahindra Bank founder Uday Kotak highlighted Anthropic's rapid rise. He noted on X: 'Anthropic, an AI company known for Claude, listed at a valuation of $ 1.5 trillion. It did not exist till ~ 5 years ago. This is more than the combined market cap of the top 10 Indian companies. Are we undervalued, or do we need to catch up in the new world? Or both?' Pai rejected the comparison and questioned why India's financial sector was not investing more heavily in innovation. He wrote: 'Bad example. Every disruption creates new cos with huge valuation. It is the nature of markets. Comparing is silly.' He then directly challenged Kotak, asking what he should do to create conditions for an Anthropic-like company in India and why Indian technology companies were starved of adequate capital. The exchange followed Anthropic's initial public offering on Wednesday, November 18, when it priced shares at $83 per share, giving the company a fully diluted valuation of approximately $1.5 trillion while raising about $81 billion; trading was scheduled to begin on Nasdaq that Thursday.
items.title: Bhalla warns India's trade deals in jeopardy amid AI valuation debate

items.summary:
Robert Reich, former US secretary of labor and UC Berkeley professor, frames Jensen Huang's resignation from Nvidia as the latest symptom of an American economy that has drifted toward authoritarianism. Huang said he would return to lead Nvidia if its board decided it was in the best interest of shareholders, employees, the company, and America; his statement cited outpourings of support from employees, investors, business partners, and customers. Reich notes that US intelligence agencies have identified one of Huang's alleged lovers as a spy for China, raising the possibility that Nvidia's most advanced AI chips may have reached China through that channel.

Reich argues that while government is usually described on an authoritarian-to-democratic continuum, economies can be too, and that the American economy has become far more concentrated in recent decades. Throughout much of the last century it was fairly democratic: decisions about what to produce and at what price reflected tens of thousands of corporate executives, managers, small-business owners, and labor unions representing over a third of private-sector workers in the 1950s.

That economy has since concentrated into a few giant corporations whose economies of scale let them spread fixed costs across many goods and services, while antitrust enforcement nearly collapsed. Reich points to union membership falling from over a third of private-sector workers in the 1950s to just 6% today as evidence.

Over roughly five years, especially in big tech, a handful of men have become both the world's richest people with significant political clout and controllers of technologies on which America and the rest of the world depend. Reich names Elon Musk, Jeff Bezos, Mark Zuckerberg, Larry Ellison, Tim Cook, and Jensen Huang as examples.

He explains this leverage through Nvidia: its value depends on Huang personally; within hours of his resignation last Thursday, stock fell 10.3% in pre-market trading, erasing about $490bn by market open, and since the leadership controversy began on 8 November the company lost roughly $800bn.

The AI industry then depends on Nvidia: it holds about 90% of global advanced-AI-chip market share and has become a major financier for the whole sector, earning some calls as the "central bank of AI." Reich notes that Nvidia's pre-November-8 value of $5tn equaled about 8% of the S&P 500.

The US economy in turn depends on the AI industry: datacenter buildouts using Nvidia chips accounted for 92% of first-quarter 2025 economic growth, and over roughly two years AI has been responsible for about half of America's overall growth. Reich adds that this leverage works in reverse too; analysts fear a collapse could burst the AI bubble and threaten the entire US or even global economy.

He grounds the chain further: most Americans' 401(k)s sit in index funds tied to the Nasdaq and S&P 500, which rest largely on ten huge corporations all connected to Nvidia that together make up about 37% of the value of the entire US stock market. Reich concludes from this leverage that Jensen Huang may be too big to fail.

Reich reports a broad campaign for his reinstatement: more than 177,000 people have signed an open letter demanding Nvidia's board bring him back while an independent investigation establishes the facts; signers reportedly include Elon Musk, Y Combinator president Garry Tan, Epic Games CEO Tim Sweeney, and thousands of self-reported Nvidia employees. Huang is discussing a possible return even though the company chair says it is not considering the move.

An ally describes a "war room" of Silicon Valley executives lobbying for his return and seeking Trump's support; one person told the Financial Times that everyone in tech outside frontier labs loves Jensen, with efforts having Huang's backing. Reich quotes Trump saying on Monday he would not mind if Huang were reinstated as CEO and thought Huang had learned a big lesson.

Reich poses two possible meanings for that lesson: whether it is simply bad optics to have an out-of-wedlock romantic relationship, or whether such a CEO should break the law by supplying America's most advanced AI chips to China through a Chinese spy. Reich notes that on Tuesday Huang agreed to appear before the House foreign affairs committee, the select committee on the Communist Party of China, and the House intelligence committee in transcribed interviews.

He closes with the question whether even in an authoritarian economy any CEO is above the law, or if this case will show otherwise.
items.title: Jensen Huang's Nvidia Resignation as a Case Study of Economic Authoritarianism

items.summary: Blue Origin, owned by Jeff Bezos, announced on Thursday that Alphabet's Google has chosen its New Glenn rocket to launch satellites under Project Suncatcher, an experiment designed to run AI systems in space. The mission is targeted for the first quarter of 2029 and would be Google's first heavy-lift flight dedicated to the project, carrying several computing satellites aboard New Glenn. Each satellite will house Google's tensor processing units, its in-house chips built to run AI programs, with a combined computing capacity roughly equal to that of a rack of servers in a conventional data center. The satellites are planned for an orbit providing near-continuous sunlight, allowing Google to test whether solar energy can support intensive space-based computing and ease pressure on terrestrial electricity grids, land use, and cooling systems. This agreement gives Blue Origin a major future mission for New Glenn as the company seeks to expand its launch business following delays and a May launchpad explosion. The initiative reflects broader industry efforts to move power-hungry AI computing beyond Earth amid growing demand driven by expanding AI use that strains ground-based infrastructure; companies including Elon Musk's SpaceX and startup Starcloud are also exploring orbital data centers. Google and Planet Labs launched the first Project Suncatcher prototype aboard a SpaceX rocket in October, with engineers reporting the satellite was operating as expected after establishing contact. That earlier mission tested whether the chips can withstand launch forces, radiation, and extreme temperatures while studying cooling methods that do not rely on airflow available on Earth. Radiation is noted to damage electronics and corrupt data, while heat from powerful chips must be released through pipes and panels rather than conventional cooling systems. Experts have cautioned that high launch costs, engineering hurdles, and limited satellite production could keep orbital data centers years away from commercial use.
items.title: Google selects Blue Origin's New Glenn for 2029 Project Suncatcher launch

items.summary:
House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries received a closed-door nomination of 251 to 11 from Democrats to become Speaker when the party regains control, with a floor vote set for Jan. 3; if successful, he would be the first Black Speaker and has pledged to fight lower costs in groceries, gas, housing and healthcare. In the Senate, minority leader Chuck Schumer faces an unopposed challenge from Chris Van Hollen, who campaigns as an anti-status-quo progressive, with that vote set for early December.

Rep. Robert Garcia, poised to chair House Oversight, sent document-preservation letters to more than a dozen Trump allies and family members ahead of January investigations into four areas: Trump family corruption, corporate corruption, DHS misconduct and the White House Epstein cover-up.

Trump, Putin and Xi Jinping met in Shenzhen on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation forum for their first trilateral summit. Their agendas diverged: Trump prioritized nuclear arms control despite Beijing's smaller stockpile; Putin sought to end the Ukraine war on Moscow's terms; and Xi aimed to position China as a stabilizing force by uniting Russia and the U.S., with NPR's Jennifer Pak noting substantial outcomes are unlikely.

Anthropic debuted on Nasdaq, raising more than $100 billion in a record IPO that valued it at around $1.5 trillion after selling 956 million shares at $83 each, above its initial target range of $70 to $78. The seven founders sold over 23 million shares, and the prospectus outlined plans for an extra $26 billion in private placements with Google, Microsoft and Nvidia. Its filing claimed AI could have a bigger economic impact than industrialization, electricity, semiconductors and the internet, with an addressable market as large as $40 trillion annually; CEO Dario Amodei has warned about losing control of AI, while political risks include its dispute with the Pentagon over model use. NPR's John Ruwitch noted that OpenAI could join Anthropic and SpaceX on the market next year.

Ben Shapiro told Morning Edition's Steve Inskeep he remains committed to his values despite disappointment in Trump's tariffs, alleged corruption and Iran war handling, arguing strict immigration policies and a White House "whiff of corruption" contributed to GOP midterm losses. Shapiro warned Republicans face an uphill road in 2028 and does not see JD Vance as the right candidate, fearing he could alienate Hispanics, working-class voters, women and college-educated Americans.

The West-Eastern Divan Orchestra, founded nearly 30 years ago by Edward Said and Daniel Barenboim to unite Middle Eastern musicians, has continued confronting political realities despite grief from Oct. 7, 2023 and the Gaza war, with longtime members crediting Barenboim for bridging cultural divides.

In other notes, Abdelrahman ElGendy won the National Book Award non-fiction prize for his memoir Huna about six years as an Egyptian political prisoner; Ella Langley won six of seven country music categories including song of the year; and NPR's Esme Nicholson sent greetings from a Berlin square featuring a Käthe Kollwitz bronze cast. The newsletter was edited by Suzanne Nuyen.
items.title: Anthropic's record IPO and Jeffries nominated as House speaker

items.summary: The annual WTO student event opened with introductory remarks from Ismaila Dieng, Director of the WTO's Information and External Relations Division, who welcomed participants and emphasized the significant value the organization places on engaging young people. Two high-level panel discussions followed, drawing speakers from WTO membership, international organizations, business, civil society, and academia. The first panel, titled "WTO rules: The basics," examined how the WTO framework keeps trade open, fair, and predictable for companies and consumers. A second panel, "Trade reform: staying ahead of the game," turned to the future, considering what policies and practices are needed to keep the WTO relevant in a rapidly evolving global environment. Between the panels, six WTO Young Professionals from the Secretariat held an informal conversation with participants, breaking down key trade topics in accessible terms and sharing their perspectives on the organization's work. In her concluding remarks, WTO Deputy Director-General Johanna Hill thanked attendees for their active engagement throughout the day while encouraging them to think critically about the discussions and harness their ideas to positively shape future trade and economic policies. The event ended with a networking reception sponsored by the World Federation of the Sporting Goods Industry (WFSGI), where participants continued exchanging views with speakers, WTO officials, and fellow students.
items.title: WTO student event highlights trade fundamentals

items.summary: The World Intellectual Property Organization and the World Trade Organization have opened applications for their joint Executive Programme on Intellectual Property Issues, aimed at senior government officials. The initiative is a collaborative effort intended to strengthen national expertise in intellectual property law and policy through a multidisciplinary approach covering topics discussed across both organizations. Over two weeks of intensive learning and knowledge exchange, participants will examine areas including intellectual property and digital trade, patents, innovation and technology transfer, and the intersection of IP with trade and health. The programme is designed for senior government officials who are responsible for IP and related policy in their countries, offering twenty places to suitably qualified candidates drawn from technical assistance beneficiaries. Applicants must demonstrate an extensive practical background in IP law, policy and practice, possess excellent English knowledge, have completed the WTO online e-Training TRIPS course or hold commensurate knowledge or professional experience, and be nominated by their government. The application deadline is 30 November 2026.
items.title: Applications open for WIPO-WTO Executive Programme on Intellectual Property Issues

items.summary: Nvidia has reportedly approached Arm chief executive Rene Haas as a candidate for its next leader, following Jensen Huang's resignation last week. The recruitment firm Heidrick & Struggles, hired by the board to find a replacement, is contacting potential candidates according to Bloomberg, and Haas—64 years old—is among those contacted. He joined Arm in 2013 and became chief executive in 2022 after seven years at Nvidia as general manager of its computing products. Huang resigned after admitting an extramarital affair with a woman accused of spying for China. Reports suggest other candidates include Nvidia vice-president Ian Buck, AMD's Lisa Su, and Apple's Johny Srouji. Arm is listed in New York but headquartered in Cambridge; it has about 500 customers worldwide including Nvidia, Apple, Samsung and Qualcomm, employs more than 7,000 staff with over 3,000 in the UK, and is now valued at $196bn as Britain's biggest tech firm. Haas told a conference in Austin that Huang was 'a legend' whose work 'is historic'. Nvidia has sought to curb speculation about Huang returning; he said on Tuesday he would be willing to return if the board decided it served shareholders, employees and America. Trump and Silicon Valley figures including Elon Musk, venture capitalists and Uber co-founder Travis Kalanick have called for his reinstatement, but chair Harvey Jones confirmed at this week's quarterly results that the board does not intend to reinstate Huang as CEO. Colette Kress was named interim CEO last week; Nvidia's Tuesday financial results showed quarterly revenue doubling from a year earlier to $115.84bn. Separately, Huang agreed on Tuesday to appear before House committees for transcribed interviews in early December and faces an SEC investigation over its China business. Both companies were approached for comment.
items.title: Arm CEO Rene Haas Approached by Nvidia's Recruiters

items.summary: The dollar eased against most major peers on Thursday, November 19, after its recent rally lost momentum ahead of AI company Anthropic's market debut. The rally had begun on November 10 when hotter-than-expected US inflation data strengthened expectations that the Federal Reserve would tighten policy further. Fed Governor Christopher Waller called for a more aggressive response to inflation, and minutes from the central bank's October 27 to 28 meeting showed policymakers increasingly concerned about additional tightening. Scotiabank chief currency strategist Shaun Osborne noted that much good news was already priced into the dollar, adding that "dollar bulls are going to need more conviction or more bullish news to drive dollar gains in the short run." He attributed part of the softer tone to a pickup in risk sentiment ahead of the Anthropic IPO. Nasdaq futures rose after Anthropic priced its offering above the marketed range, reviving optimism around AI stocks and boosting expectations for a strong debut. The dollar index reached its highest level since April 2, 2025, when President Donald Trump unveiled a sweeping tariff package that triggered a selloff in US assets. It fell 0.2 per cent to 103.65 after peaking at 103.97, while the euro rose 0.2 per cent to $1.1002. Barclays analysts argued that fiscal stimulus and strong AI-related capital spending point to a resilient US economy with higher-for-longer interest rates, all supportive of dollar strength. The gains came despite a selloff in technology shares. A Deutsche Bank tracker following more than 100 foreign-domiciled exchange-traded funds showed large dip-buying of US stocks by foreigners over the prior two weeks, described as the biggest buying spree so far this year, reinforcing the view that flows into US equities have supported the dollar. Separately, the yen slipped 0.4 per cent to 159.905, snapping a four-day losing streak; analysts said a further selloff in AI-linked assets could support it through safe-haven buying and repatriation flows, with effects likely more pronounced against other currencies than the dollar. The risk-sensitive Australian dollar was about flat after hitting an 11-month low earlier in the session, following October employment falling for a second straight month as the jobless rate climbed to a five-year high, bolstering expectations that rates have peaked. MUFG senior currency analyst Lee Hardman said the sharp hawkish repricing of Fed rate hike expectations was contributing to weakness in commodity prices and related currencies. UBS moved its forecast for the first Reserve Bank of Australia rate cut from November to August next year and extended the easing cycle to three cuts from two, citing elevated inflation and deteriorating labour and housing markets. Sterling pulled back from a 20-month high against the euro while investors remained upbeat about UK interest rates but wary of headwinds facing the single currency ahead of key European elections in 2027; the pound rose 0.1 per cent to $1.3162. In cryptocurrency markets, bitcoin rose 2.5 per cent to $63,870 from a four-month low of $62,026 touched on Sunday, aided by stronger risk appetite.
items.title: Dollar Eases as Investors Eye Anthropic IPO

items.summary: At a conference hosted by the IMF and Central Bank of Brazil in Brasília, Federal Reserve official Philip N. Jefferson discussed how central bankers should assess and confront economic shocks, noting that these issues were examined more fully in an earlier speech at Stanford University. He observed that shocks are difficult to predict and vary in length but remain familiar, citing recent examples including a pandemic, rising energy prices tied to geopolitical tensions, changes to trade policy, and technological breakthroughs. Jefferson classified shocks by whether their initial effect falls on the demand side or supply side of the economy: demand shocks affect spending without changing productive capacity, while supply shocks change potential output through effects on labor, capital, or input productivity. He explained that when a shock moves the output gap and inflation in the same direction, policy objectives align; when they move oppositely, there is a tradeoff requiring judgment about relative costs and risks. Using the recent Middle East conflict's rise in oil prices as an example of this tension, he noted it can raise inflation while weighing on real incomes and demand, with the appropriate response depending on whether inflation expectations risk becoming unanchored versus prioritizing downside employment risks. Jefferson identified artificial intelligence adoption as a particularly challenging shock that affects both aggregate supply and demand but with differential timing: business investment in data centers and computing equipment is boosting demand and putting upward pressure on inflation now, while future productivity gains could exert downward pressure on inflation while supporting growth; he also noted AI may cause job displacement yet historically similar breakthroughs have created new jobs and firms. He concluded that energy, trade, and AI shocks are unfolding simultaneously and must be weighed together to keep policy appropriately calibrated toward restoring price stability while maintaining a solid labor market in the United States.
items.title: Jefferson on Monetary Policy amid Frequent and Complex Shocks

items.summary: Anthropic made its stock market debut today, raising record sums in an offering viewed as a bellwether for the AI boom. Together with a private placement, the deal drew $107 billion and valued the firm at $1.5 trillion. The eagerly awaited opening was seen as key to reversing a recent tech downturn. Despite the strong start, Anthropic faces major challenges: sector-wide concerns over increased US regulation following Democrats' success in midterm elections, and a pullback in funding for AI infrastructure buildout. The company also carries large financial commitments to buy chips and build data centers, and must reassure customers who fear it will compete with them across sectors far beyond tech and AI.
items.title: Anthropic's Record-Breaking IPO

items.summary: Google has introduced a new privacy feature called Temporary Threads within its AI Mode, available on both mobile and desktop browsers through a global rollout. The feature lets users conduct separate temporary conversations that are kept apart from their regular search activity. According to Google, questions asked in these threads will not appear in the user's search history, functioning much like a browser's Incognito Mode. A key aspect is that this conversation data will not be used to personalize future AI responses or suggestions; when an interaction ends in Temporary Threads, Google AI will not answer based on past search patterns or preferences. The feature can be accessed by opening AI Mode and clicking the Temporary Threads icon in the top-right corner of the screen, without requiring any account setting changes or separate privacy controls to be enabled. Google says it is gradually rolling out Temporary Threads worldwide for both desktop and mobile browsers, and it will be available in all languages that Google AI Mode supports. The feature is intended for people who want information on private topics or wish to search for things they do not want later reflected in their history. However, the source notes an important limitation: while conversation activity does not appear in search history, this does not mean Temporary Threads provides fully anonymous browsing, and Google has not disclosed how long any data is retained.
items.title: Google introduces Temporary Threads privacy feature in AI Mode

items.summary: A Bank of England staff post by Dooho Shin, Danae Kyriakopoulou and Josh Perers Cook argues that the energy transition is altering both the sources and the transmission of energy inflation in the UK. Building on a 2024 report led by the Bank of England for the NGFS titled 'The green transition and the macroeconomy: a monetary policy perspective', the authors examine three channels through which changes in the energy system affect inflation over different horizons: the composition of energy spending, the relationship between gas and wholesale electricity prices, and supply-chain pressures from grid investment. The post notes that central banks historically focused on aggregate oil and gas prices but now need to understand electricity markets, grid constraints and supply chains as well. Chart 1 shows that the weight of electricity in the UK CPI has overtaken that of gas and petrol over the past decade; the 2026 weights put around 2% of average consumer spending on electricity, 1.5% on petrol and 1% on gas, with these figures depending on relative retail prices and how much heating and transport rely on each fuel. The authors expect electrification to raise electricity's importance for inflation while diminishing the role of oil and gas, including through business costs if UK industries electrify production. Chart 2 shows that in the GB spot market the correlation between gas and electricity prices has fallen rapidly since the 2022 energy crisis, whereas the futures-market correlation remains close to 1; latest pricing suggests this correlation will fall gradually toward 2030 but may change as markets roll forward, with a year earlier expecting it to fall in 2027. The higher-for-longer futures correlation is attributed to weather risk facing renewables versus gas generators. Chart 3 shows that as Contracts for Difference generation grew so did its impact on consumer bills via the CfD levy; during the 2022-23 crisis, wholesale prices exceeded fixed CfD prices and generators paid consumers the difference, reducing the inflationary effect of the gas-price shock through electricity bills. The authors note two-sided CfDs can reinforce decoupling by paying back consumers when market prices rise above fixed prices and billing more when they fall. Finally, Chart 4 highlights that grid investment pressures on critical minerals, transformers and cables could become a persistent source of inflation with broad-based impact since these inputs are also used in areas such as data centres; the IEA's Global Critical Minerals Outlook 2025 points to rising concentration in refining and growing use of export restrictions across energy-related minerals. The post concludes that monetary policymakers should pay closer attention to electricity prices, how wholesale costs are shaped, and grid supply chains, since understanding inflation in the transition will increasingly require knowledge of electrification, clean power and critical inputs. The authors disclose they work in the Bank's Climate, Sustainability and Communities Division and Content and Strategy Division respectively, and that views expressed on Bank Underground are their own and not necessarily those of the Bank or its policy committees.
items.title: Energy transition reshaping UK inflation transmission

items.summary: A public benefit corporation (PBC) is a legal framework that lets mission-driven companies pursue a stated public purpose alongside profit, giving them added protection against pushback from profit-focused shareholders. The model dates to the early 2010s and has since been adopted by more than 40 U.S. states; thousands of American companies are organized as PBCs or benefit corporations, but fewer than two dozen trade publicly, keeping the structure niche until Anthropic's market debut drew attention to it. Michael Dorff, executive director of the Lowell Milken Institute for Business Law and Policy at UCLA School of Law, compared PBC governance to "having a workout buddy," noting that the form nudges sincere companies toward their goals without obligating them. In Delaware, a PBC must send shareholders a status update only every second year, which need not be made public; shareholders can sue if they believe a company is failing to balance profit with purpose, but employees, consumers and communities have no such right. NYC Comptroller Mark Levine has said the form could help Anthropic balance safety against growth because it explicitly permits putting mission first. Patagonia, Dr. Bronner's and Warby Parker are among consumer retailers using the model; Patagonia is registered as a Benefit Corp in California with founding documents obligating environmental spending to nonprofits. Allbirds incorporated as a PBC while private to advance an environmental mission but reversed course earlier this year, showing that companies can leave the form. OpenAI's for-profit arm operates as OpenAI Group PBC under nonprofit oversight from the OpenAI Foundation, adding a second check beyond the corporate form itself; xAI was first set up in Nevada as a PBC committed to benefiting society and publishing regular updates on non-financial goals but later ended that status without announcement. Anthropic also maintains a public benefit fund tied to its own expansion, separate from the legal permission provided by its charter. The structure's enforcement runs through shareholders alone, creating tension since those same owners are limited in their ability to object to mission spending while retaining sole authority to hold the company accountable in court.
items.title: Anthropic's public benefit corporation structure explained

items.summary: The St Louis Federal Reserve now publishes a new series, the personal consumption expenditures (PCE) price index excluding energy goods, to reduce volatility in its headline inflation measure. Since January 2012, the Federal Reserve has explicitly targeted 2% inflation and measures it as the 12-month change in the headline PCE price index for its price stability mandate. Because headline indexes contain volatile components, policymakers also rely on alternative measures that better capture underlying inflationary pressures; Fed officials often cite core PCE inflation, which excludes both food and energy categories. However, excluding food, energy goods, and energy services removes a substantial share of consumption expenditures, averaging about 12% since 2012. The new index offers an alternative measure of underlying inflation that removes only energy goods from headline PCE. This preserves the smoothness of core PCE while maintaining a more representative index by removing a substantially lower share of expenditures, about 2.6% on average since 2012 instead of 12%. A recent blog post describes the case for this index in more detail. FRED now publishes the series at monthly frequency since January 1959. Comparing 12-month inflation measured by headline PCE and PCE excluding energy goods during the inflation-targeting era, the new measure is substantially less volatile than headline while preserving broad movements and trends, removing only a small share of expenditures. The graphs were created by searching FRED for "PCE excluding energy" to produce the first graph, then editing that graph to add the line for "PCE price," changing units to percent change from year ago, and adjusting the time period. The suggestion was made by Fernando Martin.
items.title: St Louis Fed publishes PCE price index excluding energy goods

items.summary:
This article is a practitioner-oriented introduction to conducting randomised controlled trials (RCTs), positioning them as the gold standard for generating credible evidence about whether development programmes work and for whom. The authors note that RCT evidence is simple to explain, showing clear graphs of what happens when people receive a programme, helps organisations learn how to improve future pilots, and appeals strongly to donors who increasingly prioritise rigorous results. They recommend building an experiment around the expansion of a programme into new communities or individuals rather than layering it onto existing operations, because this makes it easier to create a comparable control group and sidesteps ethical problems with denying service. The best time to run research is when there are clear questions about how to improve programming, after routine piloting has honed the version being studied.

The authors warn that RCTs demand tight operational control not normally required in practice; if operations bleed into control areas by pushing people toward treatment, impact appears smaller and programmes may look ineffective even when they work. Field staff are described as mission-minded professionals who may resist random assignment, so buy-in must be secured early or an experiment can go off the rails and become a waste of everyone's time. Trials also require enough sub-units willing to be randomly assigned, which for spatially large programmes means breaking operations into smaller logistical units than usual, along with long timelines from initial discussion through endline analysis.

A key concern is take-up: if a product like a loan or healthcare service isn't taken up by everyone, the only measurable effect is that of offering it rather than receiving it, and low demand can make impact look poor. The authors advise studying products and populations with high expected take-up so as not to waste an expensive method on finding nobody came. They note implementers needn't randomise their entire operation; they may exclude units too important for control or too hopeless for treatment and let researchers conduct a 'randomisation in the bubble' within an indifferent marginal group, provided there is sufficient sample size.

On research design, the article distinguishes between questions aimed at global learning versus implementer improvement. The most useful question for broad learning is whether a full-scale programme works relative to nothing using a pure control group, but this may be strategically fraught for implementers. A/B testing compares an innovation against the standard version of the programme and produces operationally useful information while carrying less reputational risk if it fails.

The piece then addresses sample size through power calculation, which determines how large a sample is needed to detect an effect of a given size, with J-PAL cited as providing more detail. The level at which assignment happens matters: individual experiments assign treatment directly to clients and have the best chance of detecting significant effects, while clustered trials must flip the coin at the group level because it isn't logistically possible to treat one member but not another within a group. Power then depends on intra-cluster correlation (ICC), measuring how similar members are relative to individuals in different groups; an ICC near zero means power comes from total individuals and matches individual trials, while higher ICCs reduce power as the minimum detectable effect rises. Using an example with monthly income of £1,000 mean and £200 standard deviation, a study of 50 individuals split evenly detects effects larger than £160 (0.8 SD), whereas 1,000 individuals detects down to £36 (0.18 SD). With 100 clusters containing 1,000 individuals total, the smallest detectable effect is 0.18 at an ICC of zero but rises to 0.215 at an ICC of 0.05 and to 0.344 at an ICC of 0.3; moving from individual assignment to group assignment with a high ICC would raise the minimum detectable effect from £36 to £69, nearly double.

The authors state that power and significance are set by convention (0.8 for power and 0.05 for significance), so implementers need only estimate the standard deviation and ICC of their chosen outcome variable using data from a similar context, decide on the minimum relevant effect size, and then assess power. Finally, they offer guidelines for productive research relationships given that few organisations have internal capacity to run clean RCTs and self-evaluation is undesirable. They recommend having hard conversations up front about operational changes needed to maintain control groups and discussing plans with field staff early; implementers typically pay all costs of the intervention itself while researchers cover survey costs, which helps avoid conflicts of interest when funding targets getting the right answer. Surveys conducted with participants should usually be done by a third party paid through the research grant rather than having field staff gather data on their own interventions, and individual participant data collected by the research firm is generally not shared because researchers are bound by Institutional Review Board constraints that independently police them.

The article also notes it has become common for researchers to file a pre-analysis plan (PAP) before starting, which registers the trial and structures analysis while documenting agreement among implementer, researcher, and survey firm on study subjects, selection methods, core outcomes, measurement approaches, and result presentation. For finding research teams without one already in place, practitioners can consult social scientists at local universities or reach out to global institutions with matchmaking processes such as the IGC, J-PAL, CEGA, or IPA.
